newsitem.title: USA: SF Fed economist sees solid growth in western U.S..
newsitem.headline: SF Fed economist sees solid growth in western U.S..

text.p: The western area of the United States, which has enjoyed buoyant economic growth recently, appears headed for continued healthy expansion, an economist with the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco said.
"I'm pretty upbeat on the regional economy," Joe Mattey, senior economist at the San Francisco Fed, told Reuters in an interview Tuesday. "I don't see any identifiable shocks on the horizon."

Speaking earlier this week, San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry also expressed optimism about the economy of the Twelfth Federal Reserve District, which includes California, Oregon, Washington, Nevada, Idaho, Arizona, Utah, Alaska and Hawaii.
"The performance of the district has really been quite good," Parry said. "I am reasonably optimistic, and what happens in the district is not inconsequential for the rest of the country."
The Twelfth District's economy makes up close to a fifth of the overall U.S. economy.

California, which has by far the largest economy in the district, has been growing since early 1993 but its expansion has picked up recently, driven by sectors such as high technology and entertainment.

Mattey pointed out that sluggish activity in the housing market, particularly in the southern part of the state, had been a drag on growth but its recent improvement could be a catalyst for further expansion.

The San Francisco Fed economist said that low costs and a perception of a high quality of life have attracted migration to four states in the district, Nevada, Idaho, Utah and Arizona, a situation that has helped propel strong growth in those states.

All four have experienced extremely rapid growth compared to the rest of the nation. Employment in Nevada, for example, surged 6.6 percent in the 12 months ended in September compared to a much more modest pace of 2.0 percent for the nation as a whole.
Mattey said he expected growth to remain on track in those states but perhaps at a somewhat more moderate pace.
"There are some signs of slowing among those western states but only from phenomenally rapid rates," he said.

In the Pacific Northwest, strong underlying fundamentals for Boeing Co following its restructuring and strength in the information technology sector bode well Washington state's economy, while in Oregon, growth may cool off a bit from a rapid pace, Mattey said.

Alaska and Hawaii have not fared as well as the rest of the district. Mattey said the discovery of new oil fields in Alaska may be one good sign for that state. Improvement in Hawaii, where the tourism industry took a hit from the slowness of California's emergence from recession and from difficulties in the real estate market, may depend on a turnaround in consumer confidence, Mattey said.
